title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings
authors: Riccardo Molteni, Minjun Jeon, Paolo Braccia, Abhinav Deshpande, Vedran Dunjko, Liang Jiang
abstract: Machine learning is widely regarded as a promising application in which quantum computing could offer a computational advantage. However, general quantum machine learning models with provable guarantees on performance, trainability, and efficient inference remain limited. In this work, we introduce quantum Hamiltonian embeddings, a supervised learning framework in which a classical training dataset is encoded into a single effective, parameterized Hamiltonian. Training optimizes the parameters of this data-dependent Hamiltonian, whose approximate ground state defines the classification rule. Once the ground state has been approximated using a quantum algorithm, inference can be performed either classically using a classical representation of the learned state, or with a quantum representation of the state. We establish efficient methods for gradient estimation and prove favorable generalization guarantees. Furthermore, under standard cryptographic assumptions, we show that Hamiltonian embeddings can realize hypothesis functions beyond the reach of efficient classical algorithms. We then demonstrate the framework at scale on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset. Together, these results establish Hamiltonian embeddings as a new framework for quantum machine learning, combining theoretical guarantees with a path for experimental investigations at scale on quantum hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum Hamiltonian embeddings encode labeled training data into a parameterized Hamiltonian whose approximate ground state defines a classifier.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports quantum training followed by classical or quantum inference, offering a route to deploying quantum-learned classifiers.
method: Encode the classical training dataset into one effective, data-dependent Hamiltonian.
Optimize Hamiltonian parameters using efficient gradient estimation.
Approximate the ground state with a quantum algorithm and use it for classification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors prove favorable generalization guarantees and conditional classical-hardness results, and demonstrate the framework on IBM Heron processors using a standard benchmark dataset.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify practical speedups or the resources needed for ground-state approximation and classical state representation.
infographic.paper_title: Supervised Learning with Quantum Hamiltonian Embeddings

title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models
authors: Andi Gu, Alek H. Kemeny, Susanne F. Yelin, Mikhail D. Lukin
abstract: Significant efforts are currently being directed toward the implementation of large-scale quantum information processors, but realizing useful quantum advantage also requires the development of efficient quantum algorithms. While for many practical problems the dominant resource costs are associated with a small set of computational primitives, optimizing them in the quantum setting presents unique challenges, including a reversibility constraint absent from ordinary classical computation. Here we introduce an evolutionary framework in which large language models (LLMs) propose circuit designs and an independent evaluator verifies and scores them. We apply this framework to tasks spanning numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, quantum simulation, and number theory. In seven of the eight tasks, the discovered circuits significantly reduce both Toffoli and qubit counts relative to the state of the art. In the eighth, the search discovers a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion. By handling reversibility differently, the architecture makes divsteps -- a classical algorithm previously impractical for reversible integer arithmetic -- viable and substantially improves the Toffoli-qubit trade-off for modular inversion. These results open the door for evaluator-guided LLM co-design of new algorithmic structures for quantum computation.

infographic.key_insight: Evaluator-guided LLM circuit search reduced both Toffoli and qubit counts on seven of eight tasks and discovered a new reversible architecture for prime-field modular inversion.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More resource-efficient reversible primitives could lower the cost of quantum algorithms across numerical computation, chemistry, optimization, simulation, and number theory.
method: Use LLMs to propose circuit designs within an evolutionary search.
Independently verify and score candidates to guide optimization.
Explore reversible architectures, including one that makes divsteps viable for modular inversion.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports significant Toffoli and qubit reductions versus the state of the art on seven tasks, plus an improved Toffoli–qubit trade-off for modular inversion on the eighth.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report hardware demonstrations or search costs, leaving practical execution benefits and optimization overhead unclear.
infographic.paper_title: Discovering state-of-the-art quantum circuits with large language models

title: Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for Solving Lindblad Master Equations
authors: Rafael Florencio Díaz, Julio Guerrero García, Elvira Romera Gutiérrez
abstract: Variational quantum algorithms have emerged as a promising approach for simulating open quantum systems, yet their expressive power and trainability remain poorly understood. We propose a variational framework for solving Lindblad master equations by minimizing a residual cost function using a compositional ansatz obtained by combining a classical neural network with a parameterized quantum circuit. The density matrix is represented through a purification on an enlarged Hilbert space, ensuring positivity, Hermiticity, and unit trace by construction, while all gradients are evaluated exactly via the parameter-shift rule. Beyond the algorithmic formulation, we derive an upper bound for the covering number of the proposed compositional model and compare it with that of purely quantum neural networks. Our analysis shows that the classical parametrization enlarges the effective hypothesis class while providing finer control over its complexity, thereby establishing a theoretical connection between expressivity, covering numbers, effective dimension, and the barren plateau phenomenon. Numerical experiments validate both the accuracy of the proposed method for representative Lindblad master equations and the theoretical predictions regarding gradient concentration. These results provide a unified variational and theoretical framework for the simulation of dissipative quantum dynamics using compositional quantum machine learning models.

infographic.key_insight: A classical neural network combined with a parameterized quantum circuit provides a variational model for Lindblad equations, linking expressivity and trainability through complexity bounds.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to modeling dissipative quantum dynamics while preserving physically valid density matrices by construction.
method: Minimize a Lindblad-equation residual using a classical–quantum compositional ansatz.
Represent density matrices through purification to ensure positivity, Hermiticity, and unit trace.
Use parameter-shift gradients and derive covering-number bounds to analyze model complexity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical experiments on representative Lindblad equations support solution accuracy and theoretical predictions about gradient concentration; the abstract gives no quantitative benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Purification requires an enlarged Hilbert space, and scalability and robustness on noisy hardware are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum-Classical Neural Networks for Solving Lindblad Master Equations

title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization
authors: Anita Weidinger, Glen Bigan Mbeng, Roeland ter Hoeven, Wolfgang Lechner
abstract: The Parity Architecture was originally introduced in the context of quantum optimization algorithms to overcome hardware connectivity constraints. Here, we show that its benefits extend beyond this role by identifying specific parity transformations that enhance the success probability of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) for optimization problems defined on hardware-native and sparse graphs. Numerical simulations suggest that this enhancement originates from the higher-order operators introduced by the Parity representation, which accelerate the propagation of correlations across the physical device. We investigate this mechanism for the Signed Max-Cut problem on 3-regular graph instances and demonstrate its practical relevance on IBM Heron quantum processors. QAOA parameters are first classically optimized on small training instances containing up to 14 vertices and subsequently transferred to larger instances executed on quantum hardware. We consider Signed Max-Cut instances of up to 40 vertices and find that, together with an error mitigation technique, the parity-based QAOA identifies the optimal solutions for all the considered 40-vertex instances, whereas the conventional QAOA fails under the same conditions.

infographic.key_insight: Higher-order parity constraints can improve QAOA success beyond connectivity benefits, with simulations suggesting faster correlation propagation as the mechanism.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Parity-based QAOA offers a hardware-demonstrated route to better optimization outcomes on sparse graphs using parameters trained on smaller instances.
method: Apply selected parity transformations to Signed Max-Cut on 3-regular graphs.
Classically optimize QAOA parameters on training instances with up to 14 vertices.
Transfer parameters to larger instances on IBM Heron processors and apply error mitigation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the tested 40-vertex instances, parity-based QAOA with error mitigation identified optimal solutions in every case, while conventional QAOA did not under the same conditions.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to the tested instances and hardware conditions; broader scalability and the implementation cost of higher-order operators remain concerns.
infographic.paper_title: Higher-order Parity Constraints for Quantum Approximate Optimization

title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor
authors: Shuwen Kan, Aaron Hoyt, Sean Garner, Ethan Vo, Adrian Harkness, Rod Rofougaran
abstract: Quantum error correction can suppress logical errors exponentially with code distance when physical noise is below threshold. Realizing this on hardware requires tight coordination among quantum gates, mid-circuit measurements, and qubit coherence. Device variation, noise asymmetry, and correlations across space and time complicate the translation of these capabilities into logical error suppression. Here, we study rotated surface-code memory on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor. Performance varies across tested processor placements, which we attribute to differences in qubit quality. We optimize the code by combining short readout, fused measurement and reset, and an XX echo on data qubits during ancilla readout. Compared with standard readout without reset or echo, the optimized syndrome extraction circuit reduces the median per-round logical error rate by factors of 3.8 in the X basis and 1.4 in the Z basis. In memory experiments of up to 150 rounds, the distance advantage weakens, alongside long-lived correlations that may reflect a persistent error component. Under our optimization recipe, increasing the protected distance from 3 to 6 while holding the other distance fixed reduces the per-round logical error rate from 0.53% to 0.24% in Z memory and from 0.52% to 0.22% in X memory. The corresponding error-suppression factors under maximum-likelihood decoding are 1.68 and 1.85. These results connect circuit compilation and optimization to surface-code memory performance and limitations, and motivate QPU and QEC circuit codesign for fault-tolerant quantum computing primitives on current cloud hardware.

infographic.key_insight: Optimized surface-code memory on a cloud-accessible IBM processor suppressed logical errors as the protected code distance increased from 3 to 6.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coordinating readout, reset, and data-qubit echo operations can improve logical memory performance on current superconducting hardware.
method: Test rotated surface-code memory across placements on an IBM Nighthawk r2 processor.
Combine short readout, fused measurement and reset, and XX echo during ancilla readout.
Evaluate distance scaling with maximum-likelihood decoding and memory experiments up to 150 rounds.

infographic.watch_item: The distance advantage weakened in longer memory experiments, while long-lived correlations suggested a possible persistent error component.
infographic.paper_title: Demonstration of Logical Error Suppression in a Surface Code Memory on a Cloud-Accessible IBM Superconducting Processor

title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost
authors: Seokhoon Jeong, Daniel K. Park
abstract: In supervised quantum machine learning with classical data, classification performance critically depends on the geometry induced by quantum data embedding. Existing data-adaptive approaches rely on pairwise fidelity evaluations between samples, which scale as $O(B^2)$ for $B$ samples and create a computational bottleneck in iterative embedding optimization. To address this issue, we propose a prototype-guided framework for efficient data-adaptive quantum embedding. Using class-prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness, we derive a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability and construct a prototype-based objective requiring only $O(B)$ fidelity evaluations. We integrate this objective into an end-to-end pipeline that combines task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous refinement of the data-embedding parameters. Across five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits, our method retains competitive quantum kernel support vector machine (SVM) performance while reducing fidelity-evaluation cost, with particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST. Geometric analyses examine how the learned embeddings relate to kernel alignment and classification margins, revealing dataset-dependent benefits and limitations. We further derive a prototype-based classifier in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space that provides an explicit witness for the SVM objective and a low-cost proxy for model selection, and extend the framework to multiple prototypes for multimodal class structures.

infographic.key_insight: Class prototypes guide quantum data-embedding optimization with O(B) fidelity evaluations for B samples, replacing O(B²) pairwise evaluations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach reduces embedding-optimization measurement costs while retaining competitive quantum kernel SVM classification performance.
method: Optimize prototype separation and sample-to-prototype compactness using a measurable lower certificate for class-ensemble distinguishability.
Combine task-specific quantum circuit architecture optimization with continuous embedding-parameter refinement.
Use a prototype-based classifier as a low-cost model-selection proxy, with multiple prototypes for multimodal classes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on five benchmark datasets with up to 20 qubits report competitive quantum kernel SVM performance and particularly strong gains over budget-matched pairwise optimization on T-MNIST.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits are dataset-dependent, and linear fidelity-evaluation scaling does not establish linear total runtime or hardware measurement cost.
infographic.paper_title: Prototype-Guided Optimization of Quantum Data Embeddings with Linear Cost

title: Quantum error correction well below the color code threshold
authors: Ali Lavasani, Adam P. Reed, Joan M. Dreiling, Annie J. Park, Michael Mills, Matteo Puviani
abstract: Quantum error correction enables scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation by suppressing logical errors exponentially with code distance once physical error rates fall below a critical threshold. Here we demonstrate below-threshold operation of triangular color codes with distances $d=3,5,$ and $7$ on Quantinuum's Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. Leveraging both circuit- and hardware- level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as $5_{-2}^{+4}\times 10^{-6}$, and demonstrate error suppression by over an order of magnitude, $Λ=12_{-2}^{+3}$, with each successive increase in code distance. Moreover, we demonstrate below threshold scaling of error rates for Clifford two-qubit randomized benchmarking circuits when encoded in $d=3,5$ color codes, achieving logical error rate of $7^{+3}_{-3}\times 10^{-5}$ per logical two-qubit Clifford at distance $5$ with a suppression factor of $Λ=9_{-3}^{+8}$. We compare logical performance for existing near-optimal algorithmic decoders, and both convolutional neural network and transformer-based neural network decoders capable of real-time decoding an order of magnitude faster than the syndrome extraction rate. These results approach the logical error rates required for megaquop-scale quantum computation and indicate that scaled trapped-ion processors could reach application-relevant performance with substantially smaller code blocks than indicated by previous results in other qubit modalities.

infographic.key_insight: Triangular color codes on Quantinuum’s Helios trapped-ion processor suppressed logical errors by more than an order of magnitude with each tested increase in code distance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Low logical error rates and fast neural-network decoding suggest a path toward fault-tolerant computation with smaller code blocks, though larger-scale operation remains to be demonstrated.
method: Tested distance-3, -5 and -7 triangular color codes with circuit- and hardware-level leakage reduction.
Evaluated encoded two-qubit Clifford randomized benchmarking at distances 3 and 5.
Compared near-optimal algorithmic decoders with convolutional and transformer neural-network decoders.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports logical error rates as low as 5 (+4/−2) × 10⁻⁶, distance-step suppression of 12 (+3/−2), and distance-5 two-qubit Clifford errors of 7 (±3) × 10⁻⁵ per logical Clifford.
infographic.watch_item: Results cover small code distances; sustained application-scale performance, including leakage control and real-time decoding at larger distances, remains unproven.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum error correction well below the color code threshold

title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians
authors: Cristian L. Cortes, Andrew J. Jenkins, William Pol, Dario Rocca, Mark Steudtner, Gian-Luca R. Anselmetti
abstract: Accurately characterizing molecular properties and reactivity often requires electronic-structure calculations across an ensemble of molecular geometries. Quantum algorithms that process such ensembles coherently could address this challenge, but they require Hamiltonian block encoding circuits that combine advanced factorization techniques with sublinear scaling in ensemble size. Here, we introduce SVD-THC, which extends tensor hypercontraction to sets of Hamiltonians defined at different nuclear geometries through a singular value decomposition of the ensemble. We use SVD-THC to construct a single multiplexed block encoding circuit for all geometries in an ensemble. We then evaluate the approach on ensembles generated by varying internal rotational coordinates in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane as well as in glycine and alanine dipeptides, corresponding to established model systems for peptide conformational landscapes, with up to 5,184 geometries. Across several resolutions of the internal-coordinate grids, the Toffoli complexity of the resulting circuits grows only weakly with the number of geometries, changing by at most 12\% over grids that differ in size by up to 576$\times$. In an energy-thresholding circuit, this yields 35--200$\times$ fewer Toffoli gates than slicing together single-geometry block encodings. This approach could help make coherent processing of molecular geometry ensembles a useful primitive for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

infographic.key_insight: SVD-THC enables a single multiplexed block encoding of molecular Hamiltonian ensembles whose Toffoli cost grows only weakly with ensemble size.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce fault-tolerant quantum computing costs for coherently exploring molecular conformations and reactivity.
method: Extend tensor hypercontraction across molecular geometries using an ensemble singular value decomposition.
Construct one multiplexed Hamiltonian block encoding for all geometries.
Evaluate resource costs for block encoding and energy thresholding.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across ensembles of up to 5,184 geometries for three molecular systems, block-encoding Toffoli costs changed by at most 12% over grids differing by up to 576×, while energy thresholding used 35–200× fewer Toffoli gates than combining single-geometry block encodings.
infographic.watch_item: The reported resource savings cover selected molecular ensembles; broader scalability and practical fault-tolerant implementation remain to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians

title: Learning angles for quantum approximate optimization
authors: Johannes Jakubik, Isabelle Wittmann, Zaheed Gaffoor, Gciniwe Simphiwe Baloyi, Craig Mahlasi, Etienne Vos
abstract: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) and its variants are leading algorithms to help solve challenging combinatorial optimization problems. QAOA maps these problems to Ising Hamiltonians such that their ground state is the desired solution. Candidate solutions are then drawn from a variational quantum circuit. The performance of QAOA hinges on a set of variational angles. However, finding good angles is an instance-specific and computationally expensive non-convex classical optimization task. Here, we learn the mapping from the problem instance to high-quality QAOA angles. Our learned models replace the per-instance optimization, that we call the solver, with a single forward pass that is several orders of magnitude faster than the solver with a near identical quality. Our models further generalize to unseen topologies such as Barabási-Albert and 2D grid graphs. Experiments on quantum hardware confirm that QAOA samples with angles produced by our open-source models are indistinguishable from solver angles. Crucially, models sensitive to the topology of the problem instance increase the quality of the QAOA angles. Our work amortizes a major bottleneck in QAOA by an up-front data generation and training cost. Importantly, this cost can be amortized over time in settings where many similar problems are optimized on a regular basis, as is often the case in applications for industry.

infographic.key_insight: Learned models predict high-quality QAOA angles in a single forward pass, replacing costly per-instance optimization with near-identical solution quality.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For repeated optimization of similar problems, angle prediction can amortize upfront data-generation and training costs while accelerating QAOA workflows.
method: Learn a mapping from problem instances to QAOA variational angles.
Replace the classical angle optimizer with model inference.
Use topology-sensitive models to improve angle quality.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports inference several orders of magnitude faster than the solver, generalization to unseen Barabási–Albert and 2D grid topologies, and hardware samples indistinguishable from those using solver angles.
infographic.watch_item: Upfront data-generation and training costs must be amortized, and generalization beyond the tested problem distributions remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Learning angles for quantum approximate optimization

title: Physics-anchored residual quantum neural networks for cloud-cover parameterization
authors: Zhuo Wang, Ce Yu, Bin Yang
abstract: Compact quantum neural networks have been explored for cloud-cover parameterization, but their predictive value depends on how physical knowledge is incorporated and which classical models provide the reference. We investigate an offline residual formulation that retains a fitted \XR\ cloud-cover estimate and learns a correction to its logit in transformed target space. Using released ICON/DYAMOND-derived data, we compare ten model variants in six- and eight-input settings, with three matched replicates and 10,000 training samples per replicate. All quantum circuits use local Z readout and noiseless exact expectation values. Under a common 30-epoch protocol, residual prediction reduced physical-space test mean squared error relative to direct QNN prediction by 54.3\% and 38.8\% for six-input XYZ and ZZXY circuits, and by 49.2\% and 38.9\% for their eight-input versions. Residual QNNs also outperformed the selected compact residual multilayer perceptron in every paired replicate. A larger, longer-trained Grundner-Q1 adaptation nevertheless achieved lower error: residual Q1 reached mean MSEs of 0.00778 and 0.00791, compared with 0.01124 and 0.01082 for residual XYZ. The results support residual prediction for compact simulated QNNs within the tested budget and establish a clear boundary set by stronger classical references. They do not establish computational quantum advantage or online climate-model skill.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-anchored residual QNNs reduced cloud-cover prediction error versus direct QNNs, but a larger, longer-trained classical model remained more accurate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Learning corrections to a fitted physical estimate can improve compact quantum models within a fixed training budget without replacing the physical baseline.
method: Retain a fitted physical cloud-cover estimate and learn a correction to its logit in transformed target space.
Compare XYZ and ZZXY quantum circuits in six- and eight-input settings using local Z readout and noiseless exact expectations.
Evaluate against compact residual MLP and larger Grundner-Q1 classical references.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ICON/DYAMOND-derived data with three matched replicates and 10,000 training samples each, residual QNNs cut test MSE by 38.8–54.3% versus direct QNNs under 30 epochs; residual Q1 achieved MSEs of 0.00778–0.00791 versus 0.01082–0.01124 for residual XYZ.
infographic.watch_item: Noiseless offline results establish neither computational quantum advantage nor online climate-model skill.
infographic.paper_title: Physics-anchored residual quantum neural networks for cloud-cover parameterization

title: Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits over Quantum Networks
authors: Yukun Yang, Himanshu Gupta
abstract: Emerging quantum networks enable distributed quantum computing (DQC) by interconnecting modest, noisy quantum processors. However, practical deployments face tight memory budgets, probabilistic entanglement generation, and decoherence, all while serving multiple users. In realistic settings -- cloud execution, iterative/interactive workloads and concurrent jobs -- circuits do not arrive in a single batch but as a stream. This creates a fundamentally online problem: the system must react to stochastic arrivals, balance latency and throughput, and remain stable under varying loads without foresight of future jobs. We study Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits (OS-DQC) and formalize the online scheduling problem for quantum networks: circuits arrive over time and must be executed without knowledge of future arrivals. At each event time (arrival or completion), the system decides which waiting circuits to launch and how to place their qubits, while accounting for congestion from in-flight circuits and constraints due to finite memories and decoherence. The objective is to minimize the mean completion time and makespan under these physical and resource constraints.

infographic.key_insight: Distributed quantum computing requires online decisions about when to launch arriving circuits and where to place their qubits, without knowing future workloads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Quantum-network schedulers must balance latency and throughput while respecting finite memory, probabilistic entanglement generation, decoherence, and competing jobs.
method: Formalize online scheduling and distribution of circuits across networked quantum processors.
At each arrival or completion, select waiting circuits to launch and assign their qubits.
Account for in-flight congestion and physical constraints while minimizing mean completion time and makespan.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes the problem formulation and objectives but reports no datasets, experimental results, or quantitative performance gains.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance remains unverified in the abstract, particularly under variable arrival loads and stochastic entanglement generation.
infographic.paper_title: Online Scheduling and Distribution of Quantum Circuits over Quantum Networks

title: Measurement-efficient energy estimator for quantum chemistry of photodynamic materials
authors: Connor Lenihan, Kripa Panchagnula, Luca Erhart, Jem Guhit, Carlo A. Gaggioli, Gabriel Greene-Diniz
abstract: Accurate modelling of chemical reaction rates requires precise correlated energy differences. Quantum computing offers a potential route to their determination, but extracting energies from quantum-prepared states can demand prohibitive sampling. We demonstrate measurement-efficient correlated energy estimation using an electronically challenging H$_2$DBB--Ru model derived from a Ru-functionalized hafnium metal-organic framework relevant to radiodynamic and photodynamic therapies. The mixed estimator combines a quantum-prepared target with sparse multiconfiguration references and recovers ground-state corrections using magnitude-only compute-uncompute measurements. Analytical variance estimates predict 1.6 mHa precision with a few hundred shots, about 100 times fewer than the single-determinant formulation and three orders of magnitude fewer than optimized Hamiltonian-term sampling. With approximate targets, it reaches comparable accuracy using simpler state preparation than direct expectation-value estimation. Emulator and trapped-ion experiments on Quantinuum Helios validate the approach up to (10,10), including a 50-qubit circuit combining AI-assisted state preparation with error detection, providing a measurement-efficient route to correlated energy differences for challenging chemical problems.

infographic.key_insight: A mixed quantum energy estimator uses sparse multiconfiguration references to sharply reduce the measurements needed for correlated energy differences in a challenging photodynamic-material model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Lower sampling costs and simpler target-state preparation could make quantum chemistry calculations for therapy-relevant materials more practical.
method: Combine a quantum-prepared target state with sparse multiconfiguration reference states.
Recover ground-state energy corrections using magnitude-only compute-uncompute measurements.
Integrate AI-assisted state preparation and error detection in a 50-qubit demonstration.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analytical variance estimates predict 1.6 mHa precision with a few hundred shots—about 100× fewer than a single-determinant formulation and 1,000× fewer than optimized Hamiltonian-term sampling—with emulator and Quantinuum Helios validation up to a (10,10) active space.
infographic.watch_item: The sampling advantages are analytically predicted; broader practical gains require accounting for reference construction, state preparation, and error-detection overhead.
infographic.paper_title: Measurement-efficient energy estimator for quantum chemistry of photodynamic materials

title: Beyond Fidelity: Resolving Errors in Photonic Seed State Generation
authors: Sara Bartolucci, Patrick Birchall, Jacob Bulmer, Sam Gartenstein, Mihir Pant, Terry Rudolph
abstract: An important aspect of many linear optical quantum computing architectures is probabilistically generating small dual-rail qubit entangled states, or seed states. While many schemes to achieve this have been discovered, attention has been primarily focused on minimizing input resources and maximizing success probability rather than establishing a detailed understanding of linear-optical error performance. In this work, we develop a framework for resolving sensitivities to physically distinct errors in linear optical state generation, allowing us to identify precise ways in which these errors affect the properties of the output state. We use this framework to identify seed state generators in which destructive many-photon interference prevents detector loss and detector noise from causing a falsely successful heralding event. We show that this effect suppresses errors, for example cutting the effective loss on the output of particular Bell state generators in half relative to a standard scheme. We also present a new Bell state generator in which both detector loss and detector noise do not affect the quality of the output Bell state to first order, and a 4GHZ generator with >75% higher success probability than a standard circuit. In addition we provide some useful identities, bounds and invariants for studying linear optical seed state generation.

infographic.key_insight: Destructive many-photon interference can suppress false heralding from detector loss and noise, improving photonic entangled-state quality beyond what fidelity alone reveals.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Error-aware seed-state design could improve the reliability of photonic quantum computing without focusing solely on resource count or generation success probability.
method: Develop a framework that separates sensitivities to physically distinct linear-optical errors.
Identify seed-state generators where interference blocks detector-induced false-success events.
Design Bell-state and four-qubit GHZ-state generators with improved error or success performance.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports halved effective output loss for particular Bell-state generators versus a standard scheme, a new Bell generator insensitive to detector loss and noise to first order, and a four-qubit GHZ generator with over 75% higher success probability than a standard circuit.
infographic.watch_item: First-order protection does not establish immunity to higher-order errors, and the abstract does not report experimental validation.
infographic.paper_title: Beyond Fidelity: Resolving Errors in Photonic Seed State Generation

title: Ground-State Sampling Correspondence between Penalty-Based and Constrained Quantum Annealing
authors: Shunta Ide, Shu Tanaka
abstract: Quantum annealing generally samples degenerate ground states with nonuniform probabilities. This unfair sampling depends on how the driver Hamiltonian couples these states near the end of annealing. For combinatorial optimization problems with a cardinality constraint, the penalty method and constrained quantum annealing (CQA) differ in these couplings. The transverse-field driver of the penalty method does not directly couple feasible ground states, whereas the fully connected XY driver of CQA couples pairs of them related by a single spin exchange. We investigate how this difference affects ground-state sampling, using closed-system simulations of random graph bipartitioning instances together with degenerate perturbation theory. For the instances studied, the conditional ground-state distribution of penalty-based quantum annealing approaches that of CQA at sufficiently large penalties and long annealing times. This convergence can be explained by the effective Hamiltonian of penalty-based quantum annealing, in which virtual single-spin flips to infeasible states generate a second-order interaction proportional to the CQA driver projected onto the feasible ground-state manifold, which is the leading term of the effective Hamiltonian of CQA. In the numerical simulations, the Jensen--Shannon divergence between the conditional ground-state distributions of penalty-based quantum annealing and CQA decreases approximately as the inverse square of the penalty-to-objective energy ratio, consistent with the perturbative analysis. This correspondence between the effective Hamiltonians extends to equal-weight fixed-magnetization constraints under the same perturbative conditions, providing a common mechanism for sampling bias in the two implementations.

infographic.key_insight: Large-penalty quantum annealing can approach the same biased ground-state sampling as constrained quantum annealing because virtual spin flips generate an effective spin-exchange interaction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This correspondence helps explain sampling bias across penalty-based and constraint-preserving implementations, but does not imply uniform sampling.
method: Compare transverse-field penalty annealing with fully connected XY constrained annealing.
Simulate random graph bipartitioning instances in a closed system.
Use degenerate perturbation theory to relate effective ground-state couplings.
infographic.evidence_signal: For the studied instances, Jensen–Shannon divergence between conditional ground-state distributions decreases approximately as the inverse square of the penalty-to-objective energy ratio at sufficiently long annealing times.
infographic.watch_item: The correspondence requires suitable perturbative conditions and long annealing times; closed-system results do not establish behavior on noisy hardware.
infographic.paper_title: Ground-State Sampling Correspondence between Penalty-Based and Constrained Quantum Annealing

title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI
authors: Tanuj Khattar, Nicholas C. Rubin, Craig Gidney, Michael Broughton, Guang Hao Low, Ryan Babbush
abstract: We discuss an effective paradigm of utilizing AI agents to better compile quantum circuits when one can constrain bottleneck subroutines to have some form of classically verifiable structure. For example, when critical subroutines are composed exclusively of reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement based uncomputation, one can efficiently simulate execution for classical inputs. This property facilitates efficient certification of approximate circuit synthesis via a form of fuzz testing, provided suitable assumptions on the input distribution. While this pattern was recently exploited to improve quantum cryptanalysis circuits, here we highlight the flexibility of the broader approach by discussing three important applications. (1) The computation of $1/\sqrt{x}$ that bottlenecks real space simulations of the Coulomb operator such as those important for modeling inertial confinement fusion reactors. (2) The decoding of Reed-Solomon codes which bottlenecks the decoded quantum interferometry algorithm when used to approximately solve the optimal polynomial intersection problem. And (3) the quantum look-up tables and controlled application of Givens rotations that bottleneck the most performant quantum algorithms for simulating chemistry in second quantization. We discuss reference implementations of these algorithms and how they can be constrained and verified in the interest of seeding a Kaggle competition designed to accelerate AI-based research into the optimization of their compilation.

infographic.key_insight: AI agents can optimize quantum circuit compilation more reliably when bottleneck subroutines have structure that supports efficient classical verification.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets compilation bottlenecks in Coulomb simulation, Reed–Solomon decoding, and quantum chemistry circuits.
method: Constrain subroutines to reversible classical logic, phasing operations, and measurement-based uncomputation.
Simulate classical inputs and use fuzz testing to check approximate circuit synthesis.
Provide reference implementations and verification constraints to seed a Kaggle optimization competition.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract discusses three application areas and reference implementations but reports no quantitative compilation improvements or benchmark results.
infographic.watch_item: Fuzz-testing certification depends on assumptions about the input distribution and should not be treated as unconditional correctness verification.
infographic.paper_title: Leveraging verifiable structure in quantum circuits to find more efficient compilations with agentic AI

title: End-to-End Optimization of Partial Fault Tolerance in Neutral-Atom Arrays
authors: Stefano Veroni, Aydin Deger, Andrew J. Daley
abstract: Fault-tolerant (FT) quantum computation offers a pathway to quantum advantage, but its realization is hindered by its significant overhead. The partially FT "STAR" architecture reduces the cost of universal computation at the price of relaxing FT requirements for non-Clifford operations, increasing exposure to hardware noise. Therefore, maximizing its performance and applicability demands careful co-design with the underlying hardware. In this work we investigate the co-design of the STAR architecture with neutral-atom platforms, connecting the underlying atomic physics to logical error modeling and application-level performance. At the physical level, we identify a favorable noise bias in $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ Rydberg gates, and show how it can be enhanced through error-selective pulse optimization. At the logical level, we identify an intrinsic error suppression mechanism, yielding vanishing logical coherent noise in leading order. Detailed circuit-level simulations of surface code implementations show more than an order of magnitude reduction in logical error relative to previous estimates. As a concrete target application, we focus on the Fermi-Hubbard model with periodic boundaries, for which we design a simulation circuit particularly suited to early implementations. We quantify the resource tradeoff of partially and fully FT approaches to gate synthesis, with the former showing approximately an order of magnitude reduction in state-injection depth, and an even larger reduction in Clifford resources. Comparing with classical and fully FT approaches, we identify regimes where partial fault tolerance provides both lower overheads and lower error rates. In our estimates, this is accessible with moderate error rates $p\sim 10^{-3}$ and a few thousand qubits, underlining that for these types of problems, partial FT approaches provide a compelling pathway to early quantum advantage.

infographic.key_insight: Co-designing partial fault tolerance with neutral-atom hardware could enable lower-overhead quantum simulation using a few thousand qubits at physical error rates near 10⁻³.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Hardware-aware pulse optimization and logical-circuit design can reduce resource costs without requiring fully fault-tolerant non-Clifford operations.
method: Identify and enhance favorable noise bias in ¹⁷¹Yb Rydberg gates through error-selective pulse optimization.
Model logical errors and evaluate surface-code implementations with circuit-level simulations.
Design periodic-boundary Fermi–Hubbard simulation circuits and compare partial versus full fault-tolerance resources.
infographic.evidence_signal: Circuit-level simulations show over 10× lower logical error than prior estimates, while resource estimates indicate roughly 10× lower state-injection depth than fully fault-tolerant gate synthesis.
infographic.watch_item: The projected benefits depend on achieving the modeled hardware noise characteristics; non-Clifford operations remain partially protected rather than fully fault tolerant.
infographic.paper_title: End-to-End Optimization of Partial Fault Tolerance in Neutral-Atom Arrays

title: Distributing Quantum Circuits Using Pre-Distributed Entanglement Pairs over Quantum Networks
authors: Yukun Yang, Ranjani G. Sundaram, Himanshu Gupta
abstract: Distributing quantum circuits across a network of quantum devices is a recent approach to improve the scalability of quantum computation. Entangled pairs of qubits distributed across network nodes are used as a communication resource for executing inter-node (remote) gates. However, establishing these entanglement pairs incurs significant latency, and doing so during the circuit's execution may lead to the decoherence of logical qubits. Instead, it may be beneficial to distribute certain entanglement pairs before the circuit is executed. Thus, we consider the problem of distributing a quantum circuit across a quantum network containing some pre-distributed entanglement pairs and seek to minimize the execution time of the circuit. We address this problem in three steps. First, given the quantum network and (optionally) a probability distribution over training circuits, we determine a set of pre-distributed entanglement pairs under a specified budget. Second, we compute a qubit-to-memory allocation that minimizes the expected execution time given these pre-distributed resources. Finally, we identify any additional entanglement pairs required during execution, generate them concurrently, and execute the circuit gates. We evaluate our methods on a broad range of benchmark circuits.

infographic.key_insight: Pre-distributing entangled qubit pairs can reduce communication delays when executing quantum circuits across networked quantum devices.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets distributed quantum execution latency and the risk of logical-qubit decoherence while waiting for remote-gate resources.
method: Select entanglement pairs to pre-distribute under a budget, optionally using a training-circuit distribution.
Optimize qubit-to-memory allocation to minimize expected execution time with the available entanglement.
Generate additional required entanglement pairs concurrently and execute circuit gates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The authors evaluate their methods on a broad range of benchmark circuits, but the abstract reports no quantitative speedups.
infographic.watch_item: Practical benefits depend on maintaining usable pre-distributed entanglement until it is needed.
infographic.paper_title: Distributing Quantum Circuits Using Pre-Distributed Entanglement Pairs over Quantum Networks

title: Quantum algorithms for optimal control: large-scale finite-horizon linear-quadratic regulation
authors: Xiajie Huang, Cristina Álvarez Yuste, Nikita Guseynov, Nana Liu, Javier González-Conde
abstract: We develop quantum algorithms for optimal control over a prescribed finite time interval (finite horizon), focusing on continuous-time linear-quadratic regulation (LQR). This foundational control problem often requires solving a nonlinear matrix Riccati equation, which can be costly for large systems and long control durations on conventional classical solvers. We instead work directly with the state-costate optimality equations, reformulating the LQR problem as a multiple-shooting linear system. Importantly, we prove a condition-number bound for the system that is independent of the horizon, under stabilizability and detectability assumptions. By incorporating the initial and final conditions into a single linear system, we can solve the subsequent linear system more efficiently with a quantum linear systems subroutine. For a given initial state, our quantum algorithms return classical estimates of the optimal cost and the optimal control inputs at a selected time, without constructing a Riccati solution operator. Given sparse-matrix block-encodings, an initial-state preparation oracle and a fixed number of control inputs, the query and gate complexities scale polylogarithmically with system size and control duration, provided that sparsity, relevant norms, and stability parameters are bounded. The dependence on the target error is inverse-linear up to logarithmic factors. We establish the required bounds uniformly in system size and duration for a family of damped mass-spring chains with two endpoint controls. Numerical experiments support the analysis.

infographic.key_insight: Quantum algorithms estimate finite-horizon LQR costs and selected-time controls with polylogarithmic scaling in system size and duration under bounded-parameter and oracle-access assumptions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could reduce computational costs for large-scale linear control problems without constructing a full Riccati solution operator.
method: Reformulate state–costate optimality equations as a multiple-shooting linear system with initial and final conditions.
Prove a horizon-independent condition-number bound under stabilizability and detectability assumptions.
Use quantum linear-system routines to obtain classical estimates of optimal cost and control inputs at a selected time.
infographic.evidence_signal: Uniform bounds are established for damped mass–spring chains with two endpoint controls, and numerical experiments support the analysis.
infographic.watch_item: Efficiency requires sparse-matrix block-encodings, initial-state preparation, bounded problem parameters, and a fixed number of controls; error dependence is inverse-linear up to logarithmic factors.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum algorithms for optimal control: large-scale finite-horizon linear-quadratic regulation

title: Local Measurement Theory for Quantum Cellular Automata
authors: Tommaso Brambilla, Alessandro Tosini, Paolo Perinotti
abstract: The formulation of quantum measurements compatible with relativistic causality is obstructed by the tension between the locality of observable algebras and the dynamical state transformations induced by measurement processes. We develop a local measurement theory for quantum cellular automata, lattices of finite-dimensional quantum systems with a causal reversible dynamics evolving in discrete time steps. Measurement processes are described by localized completely positive maps and organized into operational measurement protocols, finite non-adaptive sequences of local instruments distributed across the causal cone induced by the automaton local dynamics. Each protocol induces an effective measurement on the initial time slice, whose support is constrained by the causal structure generated by the automaton. Non-local measurement effects therefore arise through causal propagation and composition of local operations, rather than from primitive non-local interventions or instantaneous collapse prescriptions. We establish the corresponding spatial support bounds and characterize the resulting measurement architecture. As an explicit example, we construct a two-step protocol for a one-dimensional nearest-neighbour qubit automaton which, for suitable automaton parameters, realizes a Bell-basis projective measurement on two neighbouring sites after coarse-graining of the local outcomes. Away from this point, the same protocol generates a continuous family of deformed Bell measurements whose entanglement and stabilizer Rényi non-classicality can be quantified explicitly. The framework thus provides a causally consistent operator-algebraic mechanism for synthesizing spatially extended quantum measurements from strictly local operations.

infographic.key_insight: Spatially extended quantum measurements can emerge from strictly local operations composed through the causal dynamics of a quantum cellular automaton.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a causally constrained design approach for distributed measurements in lattice-based quantum simulators.
method: Represent local instruments using localized completely positive maps.
Compose finite, non-adaptive measurement protocols across the automaton’s causal cone.
Derive effective measurements and spatial support bounds on the initial time slice.
infographic.evidence_signal: An explicit two-step construction realizes a Bell-basis projective measurement at suitable parameters and deformed Bell measurements elsewhere, with quantified entanglement and stabilizer Rényi non-classicality.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides a theoretical construction, not experimental validation or an assessment of noise tolerance.
infographic.paper_title: Local Measurement Theory for Quantum Cellular Automata

title: Large Language Model Steering of Acousto-Optic Tweezer Arrays
authors: Cheng Sheng, Kai-xuan Xiao, Yin Zhang, Wen-hao Wang, Feng-yi Zhang, Xu-xing Geng
abstract: Controlling quantum hardware requires choosing and revising experimental strategies as nonlinear response, coupling, and drift limit calibration. We experimentally investigate a general-purpose large language model (LLM) as a human-in-the-loop strategy layer for a neutral-atom tweezer platform. Through step-by-step interaction with experimental feedback, the LLM guides a transition from multiplicative row--column correction to a drift-corrected local response-matrix method when separable feedback stalls. Deterministic software performs image analysis and numerical updates, while an experimentalist verifies and authorizes each waveform. For a $10\times10$ crossed-acousto-optic-deflector array, this workflow reduces the Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation from $20.30\%$ to $1.57\%$ in 30 candidate-update rounds. The experiment demonstrates feedback-informed strategy selection on a physical quantum-control subsystem, rather than direct generation of control parameters alone. These results highlight the potential of LLMs to guide control optimization across diverse quantum platforms by adaptively formulating and refining experimental strategies.

infographic.key_insight: A human-supervised LLM guided a change in calibration strategy that improved intensity uniformity in a neutral-atom tweezer array.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LLMs may support adaptive quantum-hardware calibration by selecting strategies while deterministic software computes updates and experimentalists authorize waveforms.
method: Use experimental feedback to guide step-by-step LLM strategy selection.
Switch from stalled multiplicative row–column correction to a drift-corrected local response-matrix method.
Delegate image analysis and numerical updates to deterministic software, with human verification of every waveform.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a 10×10 crossed-acousto-optic-deflector array, the workflow reduced Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation from 20.30% to 1.57% over 30 candidate-update rounds.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract demonstrates human-supervised calibration of one hardware subsystem, not autonomous control or improved quantum-computing performance.
infographic.paper_title: Large Language Model Steering of Acousto-Optic Tweezer Arrays
